title: A talker that speaks English, built small

brief.state:
Where it stands (Oct 7, 2026). B2's talker is not English. It is a hand-wired pointer system inside a 3,302,481-parameter model. It has three modes: NUM prints Python str() of an exact integer slot, WORD copies one prompt word a pointer picks, and GEN writes up to 8 characters plus EOS from 9 register vectors through a pointer-generator copy gate. The copy path adds about 50k parameters. On the six confirm seeds (200-205), pooled-5 is 73.0-74.7 (mean about 74.0), +20.3 over plain_tf and +6.9 over plain_tf_steps. PASS-1 holds; PASS-2 is still open. Forcing the copy gate to 1 costs 10-11.5 points on in_dist. The thinker-off leak is 0-10.8% (limit 5; seeds 201 and 203 fail). Brand-new families score 1.6%; the variant split scores 34.7%.

English talkers have lost every test so far. All of those tests used the older 1.2B-reader line, not B2. A 350M LFM reader and talker scored 66.1 vs 92.6 on fresh in-family questions (fails). A ~2M copy-and-gate talker on a frozen 1.17B reader scored 13.6 vs 78.2 on 384 unseen-kind questions. With the core removed it scored 12.9, so the core is not carrying answers on new kinds. Growing that English core from 9.0M to 35.8M gained +1.9 (mark +5). No sealed simple-English test set exists.

The planned English talker is stage 4b (a ~25M sentence-talker probe; its spec was due on CPU, but no spec file is in the project or code folders) and stage 9 (an open-text talker that only translates the thinker's state; pass = at least +3 over a same-size plain model, with the donor thinker alone at most 10%). Both need web text. The built slices are FineWeb-Edu grade-12-and-below from shard 0 only (12.4 / 37.2 / 117.8M GPT-2 tokens). The grade-10 plain subset is not built. Protected-panel hashes are not merged, and that check must pass before 8c. The calculator change T1 (sealed, not run) moves calls into the talker and removes NUM mode. Ben's deploy rule means the three hand renderers (str(), word slicing, reversed register decoding) must be replaced through O1 after K1.

Two traps. First, the text baseline's chain errors were mostly its 64-character answer-only cap (58 of 72 wrong rows), so training targets must never be truncated (rule 7). Second, the D0 reading probe passed (lowest place 99.997-100%), but digit writing is not yet scored; it is scored at the T1 screen.

open_questions: Scoring rule for stage 4b: the spec says sentence answers must keep B2's held-out score within 3 points, but no file says how a sentence is matched to an exact answer (string match, answer-inside-sentence, or the thinker's answer).

Source of sentence-length training text without a new teacher: the existing 1.2B rows average 18.9 tokens, and doubling needs about 60 new kinds. Whether sentence-writing by the existing 1.2B counts as the allowed teaching already run needs Ben's ruling.

Output alphabet for an open English talker: B2's talker writes from a 108-id character table, U0 keeps output as letters (BPE only on input), and no word-piece or word output vocabulary has been specified or sized against the size band.

Which sealed set will score stage 9? None is built. The English eval sets used in earlier rounds (FRESH-EN-R3, NEW-KINDS, GEN-HELDOUT) have been read by many runs and are not clean for a new sealed test.

Why does the English copy talker fail on unseen kinds even with the core removed (12.9 vs 13.6)? Is it the core not generalising, the frozen LM answering from the question, or boundary errors in the copy head? Untested; the discriminating test is not specified.
Should the talker train with the thinker or after it, with the thinker frozen? brain-talking suggests after (the thinker's score cannot be hurt); the roadmap leaves it open.
How small can a from-scratch talker be and still write fluent English? The only evidence is literature from memory (TinyStories, under about 30M); nothing measured in this project.
Should the talker share the reader's word table (brain-talking suggestion) or keep a separate output table? Untested; the 25M size plan assumes separate training.
How does a multi-word or sentence answer get re-consulted state? English copy talker scored 11.3% on multi-word spans; a sentence talker may need the core at each word (suggested, untested).
Decoding cost: the English eval and B2 generate without a KV cache, and a sentence talker multiplies decode steps. Cost per answer for a 25M sentence talker is not measured.

T1 keeps regex-found spans for the question's numbers (disclosed), and the D0 digit-writing check has not run. Whether long numbers survive the copy path is still open (place 9 of the slot path loses digits at 65-83%).
corrections: Web pool units and scope: the 12.4 / 37.2 / 117.8M figures are GPT-2 tokens from FineWeb-Edu shard 0 at grade 12 and below (DATA-POOL-PLAN section 10), not word pieces. No grade-10 plain-English slice is built, although stage 4b needs one. Protected-panel hashes are not merged.

B2 talker is described too narrowly. It has three modes: NUM (Python str() of an exact integer slot), WORD (regex-delimited prompt word), and GEN (up to 8 characters plus EOS). The current answer cap is 8 characters (data.py:11). The 35-letter and 36-register answer cap is only a planned 8a change (8A-SPEC section 17), not run.

The ~2M copy-and-gate talker was not a small system. It sat on a frozen 1.17B LFM reader and a 9.0M core (armB-report.md; verdict.md). B2's own copy path is about 50k parameters (3,302,481 vs 3,252,368).
B2 chain-5 on the six confirm seeds is 99.4-99.7 (RESULT.json). The 99.7-99.8 figure is the screen (REPORT-custom-reader-talker.md). The 99.8 figure is not in the confirm files.

The fewshot_number_rule -9 and rule_apply -6 figures come from REPORT-custom-reader-talker.md line 103, with seeds not stated. On the six confirm seeds the pooled-5 gaps to plain_tf_steps are -14.9 and -4.8 (in_dist -26.2 and -3.3).
The merged Hearer+Reader result (278.8 vs 287.0) is a bench result on the bench's own score scale, not B2 pooled-5. The bench is parked.

The 'no new teacher' rule bans new teacher models only. The existing 1.2B still supplies rows (roadmap section 1.3 item 2; section 4). Stage 4b would use it to write sentence-length answers, which is a new output format for it.
D0 is only half done. The reading probe passed on all six seeds (lowest place 99.997-100%). The writing check has not run; it is scored at the T1 screen. The orchestrator summary does not say this.

The 350M and copy-talker results are from the older English 1.2B line, not from B2 card experiments. They should not be read as evidence about B2's talker (rule 9 separation). Variant miss is 65.3% (mean exact 34.7%), a minor rounding difference from 'about 66%'.

distinct.title: CPU probe suite: where B2 loses its wrong answers
distinct.summary: One read-only script run on the saved B2 checkpoints says whether B2's misses sit in the thinker state, the mode and pointer choice, or the register-by-register writer. It fits a free readout on the 9 final registers, checks which output path (NUM, WORD, GEN) could have produced the gold answer, swaps registers versus pointers between rows, sorts wrong GEN answers by error shape, and logs per-register EOS and per-round readability. distinct.summary: B2 writes its 9 answer letters as independent argmaxes, so spelling and length cannot depend on earlier letters. Add one learned 256-vector that adds the embedding of the previous register's character (from the existing tied table) to the next register, at +256 parameters. It is the cheapest test of whether a sequential writer is needed, and it opens only if the probe suite finds wrong-length or order errors.

Teacher-forced training on gold characters (EOS then EOS fill, targets unchanged), free-run greedy decode over the model's own characters. B2 becomes 3,302,737 (margin 39,143 to the band top 3,341,880); T1 3,277,649. Cheapest variants of the same rung: one learned scalar alpha (+1 parameter). Named fallbacks if the exposure check fails: a second refine pass over the 9 registers whose input adds the mean embedding of first-pass characters (+256 with a vector, 33,632 with a rank-32 block); a register chain through a 256->64 projection (about 16.7k). distinct.summary: The planned O1a writer has no spec. Step i input = previous writer state + reader.tok[char_(i-1)] (tied); attends to the 17 final vectors and earlier writer states; readout is the existing ln_t, tied table, bias and gen_copy. Teacher-forced causal pass; free-run loop until argmax EOS or the deploy cap. 33,632 parameters: B2 = 3,336,113 (+2.82% over plain_tf, 5,767 below the band top; it cannot stack with the untie idea or any other idea over 6k). Variant S (w1d-2, on T1): replace cells() and the 9-register decode by one stream; each character gets reader.tok + reader.pos row j + stype[1] (call) or stype[2] (answer), the two segment-type rows unused in T1 (tool.py:133 reads stype[0] only; 512 dead parameters); the core CBlocks (ledger.py:102-124) run on the character sequence with a new causal flag on self-attention and the same cross-attention to the 17 thinker tokens, prompt and tape; unchanged gen_copy; EOS ends a segment; the 48-byte write cap is a world limit. Trainable count must equal T1's 3,277,393. Step B (either variant, only if step A passes): train on own72 rows with 9-35 letter answers, which requires removing the ledger.py:447 cut and english.py's 32-character drop (rule 7), and using the long-answer probe set (idea 16).

Talker: a cross-attention talker (3 blocks, d=256, about 3.26M) with a joint reader (about 0.74M) over 'F ; L'. distinct.title: Donor-contrast hinge: make a talker use its side input
distinct.summary: Train a small talker to write the first sentence of a human paragraph from the rest of the paragraph (read by the model's own reader), with one training-only hinge that charges the talker when the same sentence is nearly as likely after another paragraph's rest. This forces the words to depend on the reader state, the exact failure the old copy talker showed. It tests whether a small talker can be made to use state at all.

Loss = NLL(y|S) + 1.0 * mean over rows of max(0, 0.05*|y| - [l(y|S) - l(y|S')]), l = summed character log-probability of the first sentence y, S = reader output over the rest of the paragraph (at most 208 characters), S' = reader output over another row's rest (batch rolled by one). Talker (proposed models/sent_talker.py): decoder-only, cross-attention to S, d=256, 3 blocks, about 3.26M parameters; joint reader about 0.74M. Control = hinge weight 0. Comparator: plain decoder-only with the rest as a text prefix, d256, 5 blocks, about 4.05M (+1.2% of the whole system). Pairs: 30,933 in rung3 (rest at most 208 characters, first sentence at most 280; median first sentence 78 characters), about 93k in rung10, about 294k in rung30 (scaled). Human text only.

distinct.title: First byte of each segment decides call, answer or keep
distinct.summary: In a unified writer, the first character of each round's segment is the decision: end-of-segment means keep thinking, a marker byte starts a call written as text, any other byte starts the answer. The separate 9-class op head and 3-class mode head go, a net saving of 3,084 parameters, and the decision lives in the same stream as the text.
distinct.change: On top of the shared causal writer (idea 5 variant S). tool.py: remove the op head used for the call decision (Linear(256,9), 2,313 parameters) and the mode head (Linear(256,3), 771). Each round the writer decodes a first byte: EOS = keep (no entry); '@' = call, rest of the segment is the call text, e.g. '@add 12 5' (op names as in tool.py:39); any other byte = answer. '@' is already one of the 95 printable characters, so the vocabulary is unchanged; a unit check must confirm no gold answer begins with '@'. The outside tool loop reads the first byte, runs the calculator on a call and appends the reply as text. T1 = 3,274,309 after removal.
distinct.why: The decision is spread over three places in T1: the op head picks call or none each round, the mode head picks WORD or GEN after the loop, and tool.py:248 maps NUM rows to GEN so one mode class is dead. A first-byte decision lets the answer start at any round (the call/speak/keep token the roadmap asks for) with no new class. Suggested: a three-letter operation word is learnable as text at this size since the writer already spells short answers.

Decode: argmax over (s,e) with s<=e<s+48 inside one valid run (the prompt or one tape entry), banded search of ledger.py:368-378 over characters. Gold: all (s,e) where the stream text equals the answer (ledger.py:417-431); rows with no match stay GEN. Deleted: the word_spans slicer (tool.py:216-221). distinct.summary: Stop writing GEN answers units-first (a hand-written reversal the deploy rule names) and give each copy register a learned bonus for the prompt character right after the previous register's pick, at one scalar or a three-tap kernel (260 parameters). distinct.title: Learned choice among B2's round states
distinct.summary: B2 reads its answer only from the final state, a fixed index chosen by us, and the earlier rounds were never trained to be read. Withhold 20% of skeletons and 20% of name and noun pool words, train sentence answers from templates, and score only on rows using both withheld parts. This gives stage 9 a wording test without teacher text.
distinct.change: Using the English generator (12 kinds, at least 18,947 masked skeletons), hash each skeleton and each name/noun pool word and withhold a seeded 20% of each. Training answers: declarative sentences from per-kind templates, untruncated. Test: 1,000 rows using only withheld skeletons and words (double held-out) plus two single-held-out arms to split the effects. Plain comparator of the same size trained on the same rows. The current builder drops answers over 32 characters (english.py:13, 327-328); switch that off for this arm and report rows kept.
distinct.why: english.split_heldout takes 1% of examples and closes groups by shared passage, so training and held-out rows share skeletons and pool words; GEN-HELDOUT-R4 shares its name/noun pools with GEN by design. Current sets cannot tell wording generalisation from memory. A double held-out set of about 1,000 rows has binomial error about 1 point at p=0.9.

distinct.title: Output alphabet test: letters vs word pieces (BPE-128/308)
distinct.summary: At one fixed size (about 9.9M, tied table, same text, same updates), train four versions that differ only in the alphabet: the 108-id letter table, a 128-merge BPE learned on rung3, a 308-merge BPE learned the same way, and the sealed U0 table. The measured compression is small (1.76-1.78 characters per token), so letters are predicted to be within 0.02 bits per character of the best BPE. If a BPE wins, a 128-piece GEN output on B2 is the follow-up.
distinct.change: Tokenizer only. d368 L6 (about 9.88M for letters). Tables: 108 ids; 236 ids for BPE-128 (+47k parameters); 416 ids for BPE-308 and sealed-308 (+113k, 1.1%); all within +-3%. Windows are 256 characters (about 145 tokens for BPE arms), 64 per update, so every arm sees the same characters per update; compute per update differs and is reported. Follow-up on B2 (w1a-6), only if BPE-128 wins and U0 reports 'Ben right': the GEN readout covers 108 letter ids plus 128 piece ids (piece rows of the input table plus 128 new bias entries), a register emits one id, EOS stays the stop; merges learned on training answers and steps only; B2 = 3,335,377 (+2.8% of plain_tf, in band); the sealed 308-piece table overshoots on B2 by 39,757.
distinct.why: The sealed table was learned on skill questions, so a web-trained BPE-128 is the cleanest word-piece comparison. Compression is small, so any gain must come from the model, not shorter sequences. A talker that writes tokens needs a word-piece output head, which this test must justify. With 9 registers pieces would raise capacity from 8 letters to about 18-20 letters if the 2.31-letter ratio held (untested at 128 merges).

distinct.title: Likelihood proxy must pass a mix contrast before gating 4b
distinct.summary: A held-out web-text loss is an attractive early signal for stage 4b, and 8a's LLM arm reports it without gating. But training on more web text lowers web loss by construction, so the proxy could reward the wrong mix. Test the proxy on two arms that differ only in own-text share, with a word-shuffle control that must raise the loss; only a proxy that passes both may gate 4b.
distinct.change: Reserve one web shard's grade<=12 slice (shard 13, kept out of every pool; the 8b plan uses shards 1 and beyond, so the reservation must be written into that plan) as proxy-only text, in letters (108-id vocabulary). Train two 3M sentence-talker arms differing only in own-text share: 90% (the 10M rung mix) and 38% (the 30M mix). Score bits per character on the reserved slice and on its word-order-shuffled copy, plus slot recall on 1,000 question rows using the idea-2 referee.
distinct.why: The roadmap's mix moves from 90% own text at 10M to 38% at 30M. Prediction (suggested): the 38% arm wins on the web proxy because it trains on that text and loses on question sentences, so the proxy would pick the wrong arm. The shuffle control shows whether the proxy sees word order at all.

distinct.title: One-shot name notebook: recall a stored name without the prompt
distinct.summary: After a question is answered, store its key (pooled reader span) and its 9 answer registers as one memory slot with no weight change. A later question with the same key but no name in its prompt reads that slot so the talker can write a name it heard once. Stage 1 only checks whether the talker can decode a stored state; the learned read gate is stage 2.
distinct.change: Stage 1 (CPU, no training, no parameters): store k = the pooled key span (word_content via k_wc, ledger.py:231-237) and v = the 9 registers R. Recall: top cosine match, R' = R + v before the unchanged GEN readout. Stage 2, only if stage 1 passes: a learned read gate (256->2, 514 parameters) and a low-rank map M (256->16->256, 8,464 parameters) plus a night pass writing stored slots into M from the model's own episodes.

dropped.reason: Already answered: lesions.donor.<split>.by_family (exact, donor_match, n) is saved in every RESULT.json for seeds 200-205 (fact check verify-probe-scripts-exist). Its normalised-carry numbers (fewshot 81, seq_next 73, rule_apply 40, table_lookup 13, word_filter about 100) are kept as evidence in the probe-suite idea; only the WORD pointer-transfer arm is not saved, and it moves into that suite as the M3 swap.

Hear-back loss on a single-pass talker repeats the GEN cross-entropy (a deterministic function of the registers, so the listener carries no extra information), needs a new soft-input path in CharReader.forward, and costs about 2x per step (about 6 GPU hours for 2 seeds) with the listener-sensitivity mark untested. The version that can add information (re-read through the thinker) is kept as the hear-back idea.

Lowest prior in its set by the author's own ranking: no mechanism evidence that early letter loss competes with pointers, the related per-round supervision (Test LR) failed its stability mark, H1's warm-up already covers the useful form for the stop head, and it does nothing toward an English talker. A 3-hour screen is not worth the slot.

The 16-number variational bottleneck has a weak premise: the 37.5-nat bound (8 x ln 108) ignores that the talker also reads the prompt through the copy path, the KL on a sampled latent for a deterministic thinker state adds noise, and the question it asks (is the decision compact in the state?) is answered more cheaply by the probe suite's free-readout step and the sentence-talker's P10 vs P17 arm.

No evidence a talker needs number words (the answers and calculator replies are digits), it is blocked behind the 10M letter-LM ladder, and a hand num2words tool adds a rule-1 surface whose call rate would have to be shown to be learned. Revisit only if the sentence talker is observed failing at digit-to-word rendering.
